summary: Describes a URN namespace managed by SWIFT for use within messages that SWIFT standardizes for financial messaging. It registers the namespace so that identifiers can be written in a consistent, persistent form. It is a registration document and does not define a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Banks send each other lots of messages and need names for things inside them. This document sets aside a special name prefix, like a team jersey, so everyone knows which names belong to the SWIFT team.

questions: what is the swift urn namespace
how long are swift urns valid
subtitle: Registers the swift URN namespace so names of items in financial messages stay unique and stable.

tldr.problem: Names of items used in financial messages, such as the XML schema describing a message, must identify the resource even years after the message was exchanged.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers the URN namespace ID "swift", a flat namespace managed by SWIFT, whose names are assigned by SWIFT registration procedures and resolved by SWIFT resolvers.
tldr.outcome: SWIFT guarantees assigned URNs remain valid for 15 years and are never reassigned. Resolving them through any other resolver is error prone.

today: RFC 3615 is Informational and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why SWIFT Wants a Namespace
sections.content:
SWIFT is an industry-owned cooperative supplying secure, standardised messaging services to over 7,500 financial institutions in 199 countries. It is one of the principal standardization bodies for financial messages and services.

The goal of the namespace is stability and uniqueness of names for items used in messages between institutions. The same resource may exist in several physical locations, so several URLs, but it has only a single URN.
sections.plainLanguage: A book can sit in many libraries but has one title. A URN is the title, which stays the same even if the book moves.

sections.title: The Namespace Registration
sections.content:
The Namespace ID is swift, registered as version 1 dated 2001-08-01 to SWIFT s.c.r.l. of La Hulpe, Belgium. The namespace-specific string is a flat space with no knowable structure outside the SWIFT community's internal resolver, and nobody should infer or rely on structure externally.

The illustrative examples, which the RFC says are not guaranteed to be real, are urn:swift:xsd:epp$mi.i-2.0 and urn:swift:type:fin$103. The scope is reserved to the global financial community.
sections.plainLanguage: All the names start with swift, and nothing inside the rest of the name is meant to be decoded by outsiders.

sections.title: Assignment, Persistence and Resolution
sections.content:
SWIFT URN Registration guarantees uniqueness by tracking assigned names and comparing each proposed name to the database. If the name already exists, a new one has to be proposed. Names are never reassigned, and SWIFT URNs are guaranteed to remain valid for 15 years. Names are granted via SWIFT proprietary registration procedures, and resolved by URN resolvers run under SWIFT responsibility.

Lexical equivalence and URN syntax conformance need no special consideration, and no validation mechanism is specified.
sections.plainLanguage: SWIFT keeps the only list of names, never gives the same name twice, and promises each name keeps working for 15 years.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: Since the URNs are opaque, there are no additional security considerations beyond those of URNs in general. Resolving a SWIFT URN through a resolver other than SWIFT's is error prone and not considered authoritative. IANA registered formal URN namespace 15 to SWIFT in the registry of URN NIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask SWIFT's own lookup desk, not a random one, because only SWIFT's answers count.

references.text: Daigle, L., van Gulik, D., Iannella, R. and P. Faltstrom, "Uniform Resource Name (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms", BCP 66, RFC 3406, October 2002.
